title: Online Gambling Detection Systems: A Systematic Review
venue: F1000Research
authors: Abdul Azzam Ajhari; Aji Rizal Fathoni; Aprinaldi Jasa Mantau; Pratama Mahardhika; Jatmiko Wisnu
abstract: Background Illegal online gambling increasingly exploits websites, mobile applications, social media, messaging services, and decentralized financial infrastructure, and operators actively evade automated filtering. This review synthesizes how online gambling detection systems (OGDS) are applied, integrated, and evaluated, and which limitations constrain their deployment. Methods We searched IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, and Scopus on 9 January 2026. Peer-reviewed English-language journal and conference studies in computer science published from 2021 to 2025 and reporting measurable evaluation metrics were eligible. We appraised methodological quality using a 10-item checklist and quantified inter-reviewer agreement with Cohen’s kappa. We synthesized evidence through frequency analysis and thematic synthesis across four research questions. Results Of 1,866 records identified, we included 39 studies (kappa = 0.83). Website detection dominated the corpus (15 studies), followed by harm detection (9), social media and spam messages (6), crypto and blockchain (4), mobile applications (3), and network infrastructure (2). Researchers identified six architectural integration patterns: multimodal feature fusion, graph-structural integration, hybrid ensemble learning, transformer-based semantic systems, harm systems, and rule-based operational systems. Multimodal fusion and graph-based models reported the highest detection scores against content obfuscation, whereas lightweight rule-based tools were favored for low-resource infrastructure. Evidence quality was uneven: 12 studies lacked a baseline comparison, 27 did not release data or code, and only six reported computational cost; differing datasets and protocols preclude direct performance comparison. Four recurrent limitations emerged: data quality and temporal drift; adversarial evasion and multimodal obfuscation; semantic ambiguity of localized slang and blockchain anonymity; and computational constraints. Conclusions Research priorities include adaptive recalibration, lightweight edge deployment, deep semantic entity extraction, explainable models for legal admissibility, and Web3 forensics. Shared, longitudinal, and cross-regional benchmarks are needed before performance claims can be generalized beyond individual study settings.

title: SCARE: A Benchmark for SQL Correction and Question Answerability Classification for Reliable EHR Question Answering
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
authors: Lee, Gyubok; Chay, Woosog; Choi, Edward
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled the development of text-to-SQL models that allow clinicians to query structured data stored in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) using natural language. However, deploying these models for EHR question answering (QA) systems in safety-critical clinical environments remains challenging: incorrect SQL queries-whether caused by model errors or problematic user inputs-can undermine clinical decision-making and jeopardize patient care. While prior work has mainly focused on improving SQL generation accuracy or filtering questions before execution, there is a lack of a unified benchmark for evaluating independent post-hoc verification mechanisms (i.e., a component that inspects and validates the generated SQL before execution), which is crucial for safe deployment. To fill this gap, we introduce SCARE, a benchmark for evaluating methods that function as a post-hoc safety layer in EHR QA systems. SCARE evaluates the joint task of (1) classifying question answerability (i.e., determining whether a question is answerable, ambiguous, or unanswerable) and (2) verifying or correcting candidate SQL queries. The benchmark comprises 4,200 triples of questions, candidate SQL queries, and expected model outputs, grounded in the MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU databases. It covers a diverse set of questions and corresponding candidate SQL queries generated by seven different text-to-SQL models, ensuring a realistic and challenging evaluation. Using SCARE, we benchmark a range of approaches-from two-stage methods to agentic frameworks. Our experiments reveal a critical trade-off between question classification and SQL error correction, highlighting key challenges and outlining directions for future research.
